utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom, especially also the Russian interpreters, who managed to be here. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Pilipovic, is the Defence ready to cross-examine its next witness? And I take it that's Anatoliy Kruk?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: While that's being done --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- The Defence has indicated that DP2 will be testifying on Monday, DP2, who is under cross-examination pursuantly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What would be the status with regard to a witness whose evidence will spill over to Monday? If there is an overnight witness, would that witness be kept aside until DP2's evidence is concluded on Monday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I've been informed, Mr. DP2 will only be here on Tuesday, and we can have an agreement that if he comes on Tuesday, he can testify immediately, as soon as he arrives, depending on when we are going to work. Because I asked for that to be moved, considering that we had -- we have two more witnesses. We didn't want him to be here and wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be wise to wait with that decision until we know exactly where we stand, as I now understand, on Tuesday, if another witness would take another 15 minutes or half an hour, we might first finish with that witness. But if, for example, that would take another day, then, of course, we might give priority to -- to the witness who came for further cross-examination. So let's depend it a bit on the circumstances. Is that agreeable?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Agreeable, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kruk, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. You understand me; that's at least my conclusion at this moment in a language you -- you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I understand both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand you both understand my English and the Russian interpretation. I was informed that the solemn declaration the Rules require the witness to make at the beginning of his testimony, that you would be willing or might even prefer to make that solemn declaration in English. If you'd like it to be translated in Russian, please indicate so. If not, may I then invite you to make the solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that declaration as it appears in front of you. If you would like to do it in English, the text is in front of you. If you would like to do it in Russian, then it should be first translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I will do it in English. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Kruk, please be seated. Mr. Kruk, you'll first be examined by counsel for the Defence. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruk, good morning. I'm going to address myself to you in French, although we have always used English in our interviews. If by any chance you don't quite understand what I am saying, please do not hesitate to ask me to repeat what I'm saying again. Did you understand what I said?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Completely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And then the second introductory remark I've got to say is that I would be very grateful, as much as possible, in order to save time if you can just answer by yes or no and we will proceed very quickly. Thank you. Mr. Kruk, I'd like you to, first of all, tell the Chamber what is your background. And by that I mean educational and professional background. Can you tell us something about it, please.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, in 1990, I finished military institute of foreign languages in Moscow. And since, most of time, I worked as a military interpreter and officer on foreign relations also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Could you now tell us from which period were you professionally in contact with Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, I came to UNPROFOR mission on the 15th of January, 1993 and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm going to stop you here. But we'll come back to that, but before that--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noticed, Mr. Kruk, that you're giving your testimony in English. And you're entirely free to do that. But if you'd like to have the questions in English as well, rather than in Russian, because I can imagine that it's not easy first to hear the question in Russian and then to respond in English, there is a possibility if you'd prefer that, to have the questions that are put in French be translated to you in English. So if you'd prefer to have English rather than Russian, please indicate so and then we'll ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I'd prefer English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, to listen to the English as well. Could you then, please, Madam Usher, switch to the English channel. So now you'll hear the French of Mr. Piletta-Zanin translated into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we'll do the same as we did last time, that we'll first try to get some experience in how it works and then see whether the presence of the Russian interpreters is needed at a full-time basis or that it would be sufficient to have them stand by. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry I interrupted you, witness, but what I wanted is that if you can tell us apart from your educational experience, what has been your professional experience militarily speaking? And what I mean is your rank that you had in the military administration.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, I started as a junior lieutenant. Then I passed all ranks, military ranks. And now I am a retired lieutenant colonel. And what is concerning my professional experience -- I mean, military experience: I used to be a military interpreter in training centres in military institutions, and I have experience in my UN mission first in Sarajevo and, second, I used to be a military observer in UNTAES.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the transcript, witness, please, could you repeat very clearly the last name that you said, the UNTAES?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: UNTAES, it was former Sector East, United Nations Transition Authorisation Eastern Slavonia. This was the name of UN mission. It was from 1994 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we are going to come back to the -- to speak about Sarajevo, did you ever have an experience of the field? And for an interpreter, that is not the same thing as for a paratrooper. But have you ever had any terrain experience, field experience, in Bosnia, in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Before this mission, I did -- well, I did have combat experience. It was in Afghanistan. That's why -- I believe when I came to this mission, I got some combat experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, you told us that you were engaged in the army and in combat in Afghanistan. Can you tell us what was the length -- what was the duration of that experience, approximately of course.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, I was there two years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. During this experience that you had, witness - and I'm going to ask you a question in order to find out your knowledge of some military matters - did you have an occasion either to experience fire, that is, to be faced with the reality of daily fighting and fire, or to see the traces of fire, shooting, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: I saw both of what you mean. Fire, you mean incoming/outgoing fire, random fire and ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And this experience, did it allow you to acquire specific knowledge that made it possible for you to identify a certain weapon through your experience, to first of all say, "Here is 120-millimetre calibre," or "here is another calibre"? Have you acquired this kind of experience in the field before Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, as I said before, that I had enough experience to distinguish heavy calibre or small arm fire or mortar, tank, and -- I came with a little bit more experience than some of my French colleagues and especially Egyptian colleagues. And if I may say, that in Ukraine, when it comes to former Yugoslavia UN missions, they were trying to find quite trained and experienced people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, may I consider that your answer is that in effect, as far as the incidence of military technique firing, you consider yourself to be a man of experience? The English interpretation is not quite right as to what I wanted to say. What I mean -- what I meant by "reality of firing," I meant reality of combat and everything that that implies.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be as -- as a high-level military expert, but what is concerning general things like distinguishing the kind of fire, dealing with maps, just defining grids, and just -- I can say that in this -- in these areas of military techniques, well, I was really good trained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I interrupted you earlier because I wanted us first to hear what was your practical experience in these matters. And when you speak of your arrival in Sarajevo, so you told us the moment when you arrived in Sarajevo, and I interrupted you. But I'd like you to continue. So you arrived in Sarajevo. Could you please repeat the date, that is, the period when you arrived, and could you please tell us about -- can you tell us when did you leave Sarajevo, when did you leave Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, my team, there were five people. We came at 15th of January, spent two days in Zagreb. Then we were delivered to Sarajevo. Then we had two days of briefing in Ukrainian Battalion. And then we were assigned to our -- to our military positions in HQ Sarajevo. And exactly, I started my position in this HQ as an ops officer at 19th of January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two observations, witness: I wanted you to tell us the year first when this occurred, and also then to tell us until when you stayed there and in what capacity, and in capacities, if they have changed while you were in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, it was 1993, and I left Sarajevo on the 9th of May, because the day before, I was assigned to Ukrainian company as a chief of staff and liaison officer for separate mission in UN safe pocket Zepa. And I left Bosnia in the middle of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's still 1993, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. However, for the period that we are interested in more specifically, which is the 17th of January, 1993 to 9th of May, 1993, has there been a development or an evolution in the duties, in the tasks, that you were carrying out in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, I can say that with the system of rotation for some senior officers who were our superiors, there was some changes in operations procedures, and so actually for every month HQ Sarajevo got more and more experience and everybody was trying to just -- to make better our work, to do it more rationally and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you spoke of a team of -- consisting of five people. These people, did they stay with you throughout your mission?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, yes. Thank you. And considering that some of -- would it be possible for you to give their names? I'm not asking you to give their names, but if it was possible would you give their names?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well -- and there was Viktor Pascenko, Evgeni Kutuzov, Sidorenka, Bazil, and those are the only names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. If you do not remember, that is not that important. Thank you. Witness, can you tell us who was the sector commander? First of all, could you tell us what the sector --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. Getting the names in the right spelling on the screen always is a bit of a problem. Would it be possible that during the first break the names you just mentioned, that you write them down so that those working on the transcript will have the right spelling.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Kruk. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was the commander of the sector.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: When I came to sector Sarajevo and was assigned the ops officer, the sector commander was Egyptian general Razek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that the name can appear properly in the transcript -- yes. I believe that that can be written either with a -- with an "I" or an "E." Is that a Razik or a Razek?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to focus on your tasks at your post in Sarajevo. Could you describe for us briefly the tasks that you had. But before you do so, I'd like to put a question to you about commanding. Were there any other sector commanders during that period or just before or after that period that you knew, apart from the general?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, next sector commander who took over very soon after General Razek left the sector was a French colonel. His name is Valentine. Some people called him Valentine; some people called him Valentine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some call him Valentine, in fact. Thank you. What can you tell us about your duties? What kind of duties did you have to perform within the mission that you were assigned in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: As an ops officer, I had position first duty officer, then senior duty officer. My main tasks were, first of all, to follow the situation in sector Sarajevo, to follow all convoys, all missions conducted at that time, and to liaise with military observers, and to liaise with all battalions, as well to monitor flying situation and -- actually, all, everything that happened in Sector Sarajevo and where military personnel were involved I was following all these. And the main thing, by the end of the day I drafted a daily situation report, which was the main document, formal document, which was sent to main headquarter Zagreb and BH command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. I'm now specifically interested in the sources of information that you had in order to compile these reports. In a minute we will show you certain examples with questions. But first of all, I would like you to tell me the following: When you personally made a report which you would forward to the hierarchy, what sort of information did you have at your level; that is to say, in technical terms, where did you obtain this information from?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, during day, I had a plan of missions which were to be performed. And then when the missions were started, I followed liaison officers of battalions and other agents like UNHCR. I followed this situation and all important situations was logged in the special logbook to be included in daily situation report or to prepare some report for sector commander or chief of staff or senior operation officer. And some important from the military point of view, things like, for example, some losses in UNPROFOR personnel, it was written in official form and sent by fax from battalions or delivered by hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, did you elaborate documents -- did you compile documents which had to do with fire, with incoming fire and outgoing fire; that is to say, fire coming from Sarajevo or entering Sarajevo? Did you ever compile such documents? And if so, could you provide us with the name of the document concerned.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, one of my missions as a mission of ops officer was to monitor situation which is around PTT building where headquarter of Sector Sarajevo was stationed. And if there was nearby some incoming or outgoing fire, we had reports from our guards which were staying permanently in front of PTT. And if we saw sometimes in our window - we had a very large big window in ops room - and we saw some shelling, some explosions by our own eyes, I marked it on our operational map and what is concerning other reports from different UN sources. I received two times a day situation reports from battalions which actually -- it's the same, daily situation report, which we made in headquarter but little bit shorter, without some parts. And the main source of information concerning firing and shelling of Sarajevo, it was reports from UNMOs. It was so-called SHOOTREPs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, to clarify things, these SHOOTREPs, did they reach you because this was part of your duties? And if so, did you receive these SHOOTREPs regularly or not?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, actually, the procedure was as follows: By the end of day, we -- well, when I was on duty, I drafted daily situation report for whole sector. It was made on computer and then saved on a floppy. Then as usual, a deputy senior military observer, it was -- as far as I remember, it was, I think, Canadian -- Canadian major. He came to our office and then he took these floppy disk and then took it to his office where UNMO officer was present and then he added my situation daily report with their form, with their UNMO form, because we didn't have completely UNMO report, only this SHOOTREP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to concentrate on the level of SHOOTREP reports. In the chain of information, were these SHOOTREPs some of the first informative documents or perhaps the first such documents that were used to determine the problem of shots, the extent of the shooting, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, military observers, they had more freedom of movement than we had because they had a special status. They were unarmed, and they dealt more with local people and so on. At the same time, UNPROFOR, we were armed units, and for example, there was a different attitude of local people to our units. That's why most of times, as far as I remember, they had information which you couldn't get, for example, to send in our patrols and so. That's why we actually relied on this information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But my question hasn't perhaps been fully answered in that. What I would like to know is whether the documents prepared by the UNMOs, what we call the UNMOs, the UN military observers, did these documents -- were these documents the first documents within the chain of information? Is that the case or not? And when I say "the first documents," I'm referring to a chronological chain, of course.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, I didn't quite understand the question because the first document, does it mean it was primary document or more reliable document or ...?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: What do you mean "the chronological chain"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Naturally. I agree with you. It's a bit complicated. The notion of primary document that you mentioned is the notion I was referring to. That's what I had in mind. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: I cannot say that it was a primary document or, as you mentioned, first document. Of course, first of all, we -- our ops seniors, they had more information from our unit, and that's why there is a difference between UNMOs and UNPROFOR units, because UNMOs, they were not under controlling command of Sector Sarajevo. They only coordinated their activity. But on some operational matters, UNMOs were supposed to perform tasks which helped headquarter Sarajevo to perform its mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I have the following question that I would like to put to you now: At the level of UNMOs and at the level of SHOOTREPs, did the military observers have other documents - and I am referring to documents - on the basis of which they could prepare their own reports? Where was this and on the basis of what could they hear about this? On the basis of what they saw? On the basis of what they heard on site?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, it's very easy for me to say, because as I mentioned before, later I was a military observer and I know very well that these UNMOs had their own report where they described what was done, the logistic situation and so on, and of course cease-fire regulations. And how they registered all this cease-fire regulation: There was a special list for INCREP which is incoming report, and SHOOTREP, which is outgoing firing report. This is two forms. And when UNMO heard or saw any cease-fire violation, he was supposed to record it in this -- on this piece of paper with -- with pointing out the exact time and how did he get the information. For example, UNMO heard or UNMO seen. But all these documents, they were only on UNMO chain of command. It means all these reports by the end of day were sent to duty officer of UNMOs in headquarter Sarajevo and then reported to deputy senior -- deputy senor military observer or his operations staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. With regard to what you have described, your expression "UNMO heard or UNMO seen," I have another question that has to do with UNMO do; that is to say, once something has been heard or seen, it is reported. Very well. But is there a manner of joining information? And I have to provide you with an example now: Let's imagine that a shot falls between two military observation posts. This shot is heard by both posts. Each post will mention this shot and at the end of the day will have two shots reported by both posts, whereas there was only one shot. As a result, was there a system of verification, was this possible in order to avoid any confusion in the reports -- in the reports?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, I even can add: If there is some -- our mission going on, I mean UNPROFOR mission, and if there is some post from our UNPROFOR unit, and even these people, they have to add these events like shelling or incoming or outgoing. Of course there were confusion. But if you mean that did we check, for example, UNMO's information, how many explosions they heard or seen, we didn't do it because -- because it was not necessary and UNMOs believed to be the most reliable source of information for UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I -- may I just ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will stop you there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You added something to the question, but you did not respond to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether it was verified that one event observed by two different UNMO posts would appear not as two events, that is, observed by two posts, but whether you verified whether this actually had been one event, whether there was a system active avoiding such confusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is concerning our tasks, I mean operation officer and duty officer, we didn't verify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, as a result --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment. You said you didn't do it. Are you aware of whether it was done by anyone else or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we had such practice for our units but not UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But do you know whether the UNMOs did it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't have such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, as a result, was it technically possible if many shots fall simultaneously in places where they could be heard at the same time by several posts, would it be possible for these shots to be reported by more than one or two posts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, do you want the witness to answer the question or will I answer the question? Is it possible that it will rain next week, Mr. Piletta-Zanin? I could answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. If you allow me to intervene, what I would like to know - because I don't know; I was never there - I want to know whether in reality it's possible for three posts to hear for topographical reasons and because of the sound that is made, whether they can hear something because the sound is heard in this place. If the witness says, "No, because the posts are so distant from each other and it's impossible to hear it," then we will have clarified the problem. If the witness says, "No, because these places are so near to each other," I think this will be useful. If not, I'll move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can say only one thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Wait a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can say only one thing: According to our SUP, all units were obliged to report about any outgoing and incoming fire. And what I can say, that of course if there is a post in one unit, for example, Ukrainian Battalion who is stationed in Tito barracks, both posts can report the same outgoing and incoming fire because they are close, but it's just common logic and common sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we -- of course the witness has now answered the question. Your explanation as to the relevance of this question ignored that the fact that incoming -- that many shots fall simultaneously in places where they could be heard already says that they could be heard in different places, and your question was just about reporting, not on whether they could be heard in different places, because that was already included as a suggestion in your answer and was not what you asked the witness about. So you had just asked whether they could be heard at different places, whether they could be reported as more incidents. And I would say that we asked the witness to answer that question but it's a question that everyone could answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll move on to a question that can't be answered by everyone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Who has heard the testimony of the earlier witness and who has some sense of logic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in purely logical terms and given the layout of the ground and the structure of Sarajevo which we do not know as well as you do, the phenomenon of an echo, is this a phenomenon which would occur in reality? And I am referring to areas where there are high-rise buildings in particular. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object. It's a hypothetical question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has nothing hypothetical about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Mr. Piletta-Zanin asked the witness is whether in the circumstances as you find them in Sarajevo, whether the witness has the experience that echoes would be heard, and I take it that you are asking about echoes of the sound of firing, or are you interested to know about anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've heard what you said, Mr. President. I've understood you. My question has to do with the reality of the phenomenon in Sarajevo and the possible consequences that it could have. That's the second part with regard to calculations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Question, because I -- the question was whether the phenomenon of an echo would occur in reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. May I just ask you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you are interested to know about the echoes of the -- of what? Of people singing? I take it that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The echo of my voice is not very interesting. What I'm interested in is the echo of -- of a shot, as it is landing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin has asked whether you experienced the phenomenon of an echo to occur when a shell was falling.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of course, there was phenomenon of echo, and I can say yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the next question, which logically comes out of that, is whether this phenomenon of echo -- firstly, was it frequent? And secondly, was it something that may have caused errors in the reports compiled, made by the observers?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Inviting the witness to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, may I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to get an answer on the first question that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it frequent?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The echo.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, of course it was better to ask people who were outside on the missions, because most of time I spent in PTT. Only maybe four or five times I visited battalion, and I heard by myself this echo for incoming shots and so. But of course it depends on the area where it happened, if there is a high-rise buildings or it's a summer house. Is it -- it depends on the area, the kind of structures and so just there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you cannot say about the frequency because you were not in the field, you were not on the ground. But on the principle of the existence of the echo, did you ever hear it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. I think the witness has already answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has answered that question that he experienced the phenomenon of echo but that he could not tell much about the frequency because he was usually indoors.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this kind -- in a sense that you've had this experience, this kind of echo, was this likely to cause errors in the reports?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me ask you, Mr. Kruk, do you have any experience or any knowledge of such echoes causing errors in reporting either incoming or outgoing fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have such experience, but there was some -- some mistakes in the reporting from battalions, but I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that caused --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This position doesn't relate to this, to echo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not to echo. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to echo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, considering that the witness told us there were errors, could we please have the exhibit. I gave the list to Madam Registrar the other day, and this is exhibits that were under seal, I believe. So it would be good if they were not placed on the ELMO. And this is 918, 925, and 932.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, witness, could you please look at these documents once they are in front of you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. [In English] Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Chamber might have some difficulties in following the testimony if the document is not on the ELMO because I noticed that there was a long -- a very long list with ERN numbers, and am I right that it is -- do I find the P numbers somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: P number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is that at the top of the document, I think?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, but on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: On the list? I don't have the list on me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, the Chamber, of course, tries to prepare itself on the -- what it can expect. And if I would know that there were some admitted pieces in evidence, then we could prepare ourselves on it. And for example, I take it now -- we cannot follow the testimony of the witness if it's not on the ELMO and if we have no copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I would agree with you. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't expect you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Closed session. Yes, of course, but we should not turn into closed session unless it is necessary. But let's now turn into closed session so that the documents can be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you spoke of battalions earlier. Could you please tell us precisely to which battalion were you referring. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: At my time there were three battalions: French Battalion stationed in airport; Ukrainian Battalion was stationed in Tito barracks; and Egyptian Battalion was stationed in Bistrik barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have close contact with these battalions, and more specifically with the Ukrainian Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, of course, because I was Ukrainian officer I had more close contacts with Ukrainian Battalion, and I had good contacts with other battalions as well, because in our ops room, as I mentioned before, there were present all liaison officers from all battalions just to be in touch with battalions at any time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you remind us, where was the battalion in question? Where was it located?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: What battalion do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Ukrainian Battalion.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: The Ukrainian Battalion was stationed in so-called Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you are speaking about the Tito barracks, can you tell us something about the presence of armed elements, I mean in the most general sense, in the Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: In Tito barracks, there was UN camp where was stationed Ukrainian Battalion and Dutch communications centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I was not speaking about the presence of UN elements, parts of the UN structure in my question, but I was speaking in general. Were there any other, apart from the personnel, armed or not, of the UN, was there any other armed elements of other parties inside within the compound of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: As far as I was told by Ukrainian officers from the Ukrainian Battalion, part of Tito barracks were not engaged -- were occupied by some logistic branch of BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can you inform us in which part of the barracks was your answer referring to.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, our UN camp was separated from that part of Tito barracks. We occupied two buildings in this barracks, and there was a fence and there was another territory which didn't belong to UN camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. This situation, did it last throughout your stay?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, could we now go on to another subject, and we'll now talk about life in that part of Sarajevo that remained under the control of the BH forces. And the first question that I have in mind in relation to that is that: Did you have any free time? And if so, what did you do during your free time, that is, when you were not inside the compound of the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Because we had only three officers in our duty shift, that's why I almost didn't have free time. And if I had, I used it for -- for recreation, because it was very tense work with a big operation and so on. That's why I didn't go very often to Ukrainian Battalion. But I did remember I went there four -- four or five times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But did it ever happen to you that you went to other sectors of the city, apart from the one where the Tito barracks were?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: I went two times to airport -- correction, three times, three times to airport. And once I went to engineer mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is not during your free time. But can you tell us, from where -- no, I'm sorry, where?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Where did I go?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go for that technical mission?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: I don't remember the area of Sarajevo. It was only once or maybe two times. But if I see my reports after this engineer mission, which I believe were included in daily situation report, I would say it exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us stop here about that mission. In relation to this mission, did anything specific occur during this technical mission?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I was mission commander and I had escort commander. He was a Canadian lieutenant. Unfortunately I didn't remember his name. And once we came under fire on the way to this mission, and then there was exchange of fire on the place of mission and the mission was cancelled due to security reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if I would put the following question to the witness, could you please tell me whether that would assist you. The question would be: Did you ever spend any time when you were not on duty in the city, and would you have an opportunity to observe the daily life of the citizens? Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Absolutely. But you have estimated the situation perfectly well, but you have also seen that for the moment I decided to see what happened at this technical mission and then later on I would gladly go on to that question after I found out what happened to the mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would put that question later on in this way, then you might get the answer you would like to have. And I'm just suggesting how to get the answers I take it you would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, please bear in mind the perfectly phrased question that the President asked. We will come back to it. But now logically, I will have to proceed in this way: What happened during this mission you were fired at? And my question is the following: Were you able to establish where the shots came from?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, we were very close to confrontation line, and what side fired on us, I cannot say for sure. First of all, we were moving in Canadian APC inside, and well, we only heard the ricochet from our APC. So I cannot say exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without projecting anything whatsoever, do you know why would anybody fire at you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. Inviting the witness to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. I -- I just asked the witness whether he knew if there was an investigation into the causes, then yes. If he doesn't know, he doesn't know. He can say he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then ask whether it was investigated, what were the results of the investigations rather than ask it in this way: Ask, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, for facts, rather than asking for --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to save time, Mr. President. But very well. I will do this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Has there been an investigation following this event?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no investigation. It was the usual case for Sarajevo at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I am going on to another subject now. I asked you to remember the question that the President asked earlier, and I would even add something to it, that is, did you go into the old town?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question is whether when you were not on duty whether you would spend any time in the old town and whether you were able to observe the daily life of citizens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't have any chance to go for -- for a walk or just for -- for travelling or for seeing sights. Just only for, if it's needed, I went to battalion, as I said before, four or five times, and that's all. First of all, it was not allowed for us to leave PTT, even just not to go outside -- outside the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I will stop you here for -- in order not to waste time. Thank you. When you moved inside the town, when you -- during your movements inside the town, did you have an opportunity to see in the city or elsewhere soldiers belonging to the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object. The witness has already answered that he did not go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not so. He said that he did not have time to go outside during his free time and that it was forbidden, but he did say that he moved twice or -- well, if I cannot be heard, then very well. I will take note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can answer this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I first ask you: Did you ever move into the town when you were on duty, apart from what you just told us, going to the battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. As I said before, I went to engineer mission I can believe it was in town. And of course going to battalion as well could be included. And if the point of question, did I see people in military uniform, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, what I -- why I intervened is that it becomes confusing if we do not know exactly what facts the witness is testifying about. I'm not excluding that he went to town when he was not on duty, but you suggested it, where we do not know it yet. So if you systematically put your questions to the witness, we'll get as many answers as possible, and that's what the Chamber really would like, to hear the answers rather than to hear about confusion in questioning. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. To be precise in the interest of the matter, the witness said what I wanted to say equally was that he went three times also to the airport and that,, not to one battalion but battalions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you moved about inside the city, you told us that you saw soldiers in uniform. What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I saw once three men leaving a civilian car. They were in camouflage. It was next to Ukrainian Battalion. And as well, when I was on engineer mission, there was maybe six or eight people. Some of them were half in camouflage, half in civilian clothes, but they had weapon, and it was just next to confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a few clarifications in relation to facts. You spoke of a civilian car. Can you tell us what type of vehicle was that?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, it was usual civilian vehicle, like for usual driving. We call it soft skin vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And so if that car was a civilian vehicle, was there any -- did it have any other distinguishing features that another car that was not used by the army would not have?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: No. The only passengers were in camouflage uniform and armed with small arms and that's all. No special about this vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's time for a break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did not hear the last words of the witness, as a matter of fact. What was the last words you spoke, Mr. Kruk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I added that maybe it was a little bit rusted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Rusted, yes. I don't know whether this is a military feature or not or a civilian feature. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to continue the examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I would like to thank the registrar. It has been copied, I think. And I spent a significant part of the break to photocopy a document with a machine that wasn't functioning quite properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Mr. President, whether your Chamber already has the three documents that I mentioned earlier on just a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we have not received them yet. We now do receive them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do have many copies. We have additional copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you provide the additional copies to the booth, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But I will do so gladly. I'll do that immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, Ms. Mahindaratne, to keep a close eye on what exactly the protected information would be in the document. It will not be put on the ELMO. And if it's just about the structure of this kind of documents, we've seen such documents before. I don't think there is any need to specifically protect the structure of the document. And would you also keep in mind, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that whenever we touch upon a point which might be sensitive that we turn into closed session. Then please proceed. The document is not to be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in order to use the time as best as possible, while this document is being provided to the booths, I'll ask the witness some other questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, with regard to the PTT building in Sarajevo and the surrounding area - and I'm referring to the parameter of the building, the surroundings of the building - what can you tell us about this, please?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: The PTT building, it was a highscraper where four stages were occupied by UN personnel, and it had two stages down, and a basement and so. Our living room was facing two blocks of flats, and in front of our room was a road, and nearby was a small river, and this is geographic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But my question did not really have to do with the geography, but I will be more precise. What can you tell us about the building's parameter, the PTT building's parameter? And I mean, it's possible -- the legal character, was there a certain zone which made it possible to distinguish it from other zones around the PTT building? Was there a certain legal zone?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: The PTT had walls made from sandbags. That's why if you see it, it had a -- like a white band. It was distinguishable from --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the orders that you received or in the administrative instructions that you had, was there anything that said that something could or could not be done within a certain parameter surrounding the so-called PTT building? Did it define in this sense a zone surrounding it? Have you understood the question?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. First of all, according to standard procedures, any of UN personnel couldn't leave PTT without flak jacket and helmet, what is concern UN personnel. And according to UN rules and there was a zone of 500 metres which were not permitted for any warring parties to be present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, since you mentioned this zone of 500 metres, I have two questions: Was a diameter or a sort of area -- no, a diameter or a range. For the English translation, not range. It would sooner be radius, I think. Thank you. How were these 500 metres calculated?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, easily to explain, it was 500 metres from sandbags or from fence which was around PTT, and it was -- it could be designed visually. There was no special measuring, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But would you agree with me in considering this as a global zone of 1.000 metres on both sides of the building, 500 metres to the east and 500 metres to the west? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Yes, this is 500 metres from the wall to west, east, north, and ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So we're speaking about a radius of 500 metres. Why was this zone there, and what was it called?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, it was a safe zone for UN, just to protect UN personnel from shelling, from firing and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Nevertheless, did you ever personally hear shots that had been fired from this area? Did you hear these shots?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Two times I do remember that when there was a severe violation from Bosnia side, when they penetrated to this zone and made a couple of shots. The first time, I remember it very well because there was a small table tennis championship. And when we started to play - I don't remember for what place and -- in coffee room - and there was two outgoing shots. And in -- very soon there was retaliation, and even a couple of sandbags just fell down this coffee room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, why did these shots -- why did these outgoing shots occur? Or as you said, there was a security zone -- around the building? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. Inviting the witness to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to know whether the witness knew or did not know, not whether he was imagining something. It's nothing that he has to speculate about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, you may answer that question. And please do it in such a way that the Chamber will know what's the basis of your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I mentioned before, at that time not only me - there was maybe tens of people in coffee room - and we heard -- I personally heard outgoing shots from mortar, and I can say it was mortar 82 millimetres approximately, according to the sound. And everybody was very angry about this because it was strictly prohibited to provocate near UN camp because it can endanger UN personnel. It always was very strong protest from headquarter Sarajevo. And I do remember two times in the headquarter it happened and once it was during my engineer mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But the question was whether you knew the reasons for which these shots had been provoked. If you don't, you can just say that you don't.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: I can say that -- and I will tell common opinion of the people who were present there. It was pure provocation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For what purpose?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Maybe to -- to receive backfire, and in this case to make opposing side to be guilty for these might-be casualties or destruction for UN.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, this security zone that you have spoken about, the radius of which was 500 metres, was it also used for other military buildings used by the UN forces, such as, for example, observation posts?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: It was a general rule for all UN positions, for all UN camps and so where UN personnel present permanently there was this security zone, 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to be as precise as possible. Does your answer as a result include the observation posts that we know are sometimes located in normal houses? Did your answer also refer to these posts?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly what was concerning UNMO's observation post because sometimes they moved from one post to another, but I think this rule was -- was used for any UN position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you personally know about other provocative situations that might have occurred at sites other than that of the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, as I mentioned before, during engineering mission when we came at the place where repair workers were supposed to be started, there came five or six people armed and there was a -- some exchange of words between local workers, and this is so-called words, and then there was outgoing firing from small arm fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, we are now going to be examining some documents. First of all, I would like to ask you whether you recognise each of the three documents, and then I will move on to more specific questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, first of all, could you have a look at the first document, bearing the number 925. Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It's P925 at the very top.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may just point out, this is a Rule 70 document and it has not been cleared, as well as Witness Y, who is a protected witness, his name is on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's first of all the reason why I said that it could not be put on the ELMO. If, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't have any questions, Mr. President, including those -- including names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Including names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But I would say the information in the document as such is protected. So therefore, we should then deal with it in closed session, unless the questions are of such a general nature that they would not jeopardise in whatever way -- if, for example -- let me just assume, say, well, we read the word "Howitzer." In the document. Could you tell us what a Howitzer is. That would not reveal anything, I would say, would be protected. But as soon as it comes to the content -- or if, for example, you would ask about the system of reporting, that's fine. But as soon as we come to the content of the document itself, whether names or other events, we should respect the -- we should respect the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in order not to waste time, will the Prosecution tell me what its position is in relation to the two other documents with regard to this question concerning confidential information.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: With regard to those two documents, Mr. President, the Rule 70 has been cleared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that's only 925 that is --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And 925, in order to avoid whatever problem, while copying -- specifically the number, what I take to be 925 at the top, is only half copied. But let's talk about 918, 932, and then the third one we all consider that to be 925.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in an abundance of caution, since all three documents have been tendered under seal, perhaps if evidence is dealt with with regard that these three document, we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we don't put it on the ELMO and go into private session, that would perhaps be the best solution. Let's in order to work as efficiently as possible go into private session and let's keep in mind that as soon as it's not necessary anymore, to go into open session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put it to you in a different way: In the case of incoming rounds, there are factors such as sound, smoke, and perhaps the field of vibration which are factors which would assist UNMO to observe the incoming round. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the case of outgoing rounds, there is no smoke.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Obviously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And perhaps the field of vibration is not as much as in the case of an incoming round?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, it's not as in -- even former military, just -- I only can repeat it. It depends on the distance. For example, if you even heard what a tank fires and what is an explosion, for example, anti-aircraft calibre shots, it's a big difference. Well, it's -- if we say of specific case with distances. But generally it's -- we have to follow the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you consider that all these elements the distances were the same with regard to an incoming round as well as an outgoing round, would you not agree with me that factors such as sound, smoke, and the feel of the vibration assists one in monitoring or observing an incoming round much better than an outgoing round?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Okay. Finally I understood what you're asking me. Well, of course. For all this is three parameters, like smoke, like just light, when it's explosion, and vibration. Of course, it's more easily could be observed by anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Additionally wasn't it the case - of course, the documents have now been removed from your table - but wasn't it the case that the documents itself in the first paragraph explained the reasons for the -- the fact that -- as to why the incoming rounds and the outgoing rounds did not correspond to each other? Did you read the first paragraph, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Yes. And I read the first paragraph and the last paragraph, and there is excuse that that's why these figures don't maybe correspond the figure of outgoing and incoming. And at the end of this SHOOTREP, there's an excuse for maybe not a high accuracy of all the numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke of an incident when you went on an engineering mission where some people had -- got involved in a shooting incident after an argument.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: There was no argument. Well, if I described maybe in some details. When we came on the place, where five or six people came with arms, they greeted workers -- local workers who came with me, and Canadian escort officer and soldiers, me as well, and then we were about to start our mission. Very close, maybe 50 metres from us, there was small arms fire, outgoing fire. I can say it was automatic rifle exactly. And then in -- very soon we had back -- how can I say -- retaliation from opposite side. It was a mortar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the location?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: No, I don't remember exactly the location. But if I see the situation report and my report when I drew after I came from this mission and -- well, I would tell exactly what was the location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it at the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Yes, it was very close to confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On which territory? On territory held by the Bosnian army or the --

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: The Bosnian army. Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke of a Ukrainian officer informing you that part of the Tito barracks was occupied by the logistic branch of the BH army. Can you identify that person who told you this. Do you remember the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: It was not only one but many Ukrainian officers, because they lived there every day. They communicated with local people. And that's why they were there for me a source of information. And I can just name any company commander or platoon commander and so on. If you need -- Albert Bondarchuk. Who else? Vorchak, Vladimir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: I can name you maybe all officers if I had a list and -- everybody knew it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which part of the building was this? Was it on the -- the north, the east, the west, or the south?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: If I see the sketch of this place -- but as I mentioned before, there was two -- two buildings occupied by Dutch concern and our battalion. And then there was a fence and there was another territory, and I was told there was some logistical element.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may assist you in trying to ascertain the direction. You know the -- the road referred to as the sniper alley, which goes from east to west or west to east through the city?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Yes. This is the main street which we used to go from Ukrainian Battalion to PTT.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you take the side of the Tito barracks which faces sniper alley as south, now would you be able to tell me on which side this logistic branch was, whether it was the north, the south, the east, or the west?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, I still be more sure if I had a sketch of this territory and so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your permission, just to assist the witness to get the direction, if I may just show a map which has been used right through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may. And would you use as neutral names as possible for streets you want to describe.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. May I have that back. I don't think that is an appropriate map to show, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could you perhaps -- it's a very small area, I would say. Could you make sure that you have a suitable map after the break and then put that question to the witness and now proceed with other matters --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that you have 20 minutes to make the right cut of the map you would need.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that would be my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, it would be your last question. Well, we could really do two things right now. But if you have a good map that really suits your purpose, then you could do it now. Otherwise -- we have a -- we very often use a coloured map which covers the whole city and -- I don't think that's the one you have in your hands by now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I have the coloured map, Mr. President. It's just that I've made some markings and it would the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. You should use a clean one. Perhaps we could -- even if it would be the last question, perhaps better have the break now and you take a good map, perhaps enlarge the part you need during the break, and we'll then resume at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it would be -- Mr. Kruk, we expect that you'd be here only briefly after that. It depends on whether there are any additional questions to be put to you. But we'll first adjourn so that the Prosecution is able to prepare a proper map that you could use, and we'll then resume at twenty-five minutes to 1.00 and then have no further break any more and continue until 1.45. Yes. We'll adjourn until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, did you manage to get the map?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. But of course it's not -- it does not show the Tito barracks in a larger scale. I just merely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see how far we come with this map, and perhaps that could then be put on the ELMO --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- When you ask the witness questions about it. Could then the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Usher. Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I may have the assistance of the usher just to place the map, this area, on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you could zoom in on the ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you identify the Tito barracks on this map?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: There is not good light.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The map may be moved to the right a little perhaps. The map can be moved to the right and the camera zoom in on the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I take it that you don't have copies -- copies for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Within the time period I had, I couldn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am sorry to interrupt, but we have a number of copies here that we will gladly give for the disposal of everyone. And on this map you can also see the barracks. With great pleasure, the Defence will offer copies to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm thankful to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that's a copy of the same map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a tourist plan of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will certainly assist us to have the map. If it's be enlarged, it might even be given to the witness if this is an enlarged part. If not, then ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but Your Honour, I was planning to use this map for the examination of the next witness. I can provide it to be used now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There will not be markings on this map, just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There will be no markings. So we'll return it to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If the cameras could zoom in on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify Tito barracks on the map, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, if -- if I am not mistaken, I think this is Tito barracks on the left side of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could perhaps that part of the map that the witness just pointed at be put in the centre of the map and that the witness again indicates. Yes. Could you -- could you again point at it, Mr. Kruk.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this is the Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you examine that area and indicate as to on which side or which part of the barracks was the logistic branch of the BH.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, I can say that -- that the entry of our -- just not our -- Ukrainian Battalion was stationed at Tito barracks. There was one building here there was three companies, and Dutch com centre. And here was headquarter. And there was after fence as -- well, actually, I was told that after -- after -- next to barracks there is another barracks which were occupied. But you have to understand, I was only four times driving by APC, and what I was interested just to visit some of people and our officer mess and that's all, and all I can describe, the UN camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I take it then that you yourself personally did not see or do not know --

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- As to whether there was in fact the logistic branch of the BH army located at this premises. You can only speak of what has been told to you.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Yes, of course. As I mentioned before, I was told by a local officer -- I mean Ukrainian officers, because they lived there. They knew the area much better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You cannot say even on which side of this complex the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may finish my question.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of this complex the logistic branch was located at.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: I know that it was next to the UN camp where Ukrainian Battalion was stationed. And I only remember how building where our units were were situated on this territory. And -- and what was going on behind the fence which were surrounded Ukrainian Battalion, well, I cannot say exactly. Only from words which I heard from our officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
