utterances.text: When you use the word "behind," are you referring to the northern side of the complex? When you say "behind," it's behind from the direction you're looking at, this map, would you say the side on the north?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: I think where was end of building where was headquarter of our company. There was continuation of building. Maybe there was the element of -- of BH army. But I am not sure. First of all, it's ten years past, and I was driving there only four or five times. And I was not interested in this information, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one last question.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: It only -- for me it was general information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one last question on this: On which side was the Ukrainian Battalion located? On the northern side?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of the transcript, perhaps before the witness answers this question, it would be very useful to indicate that just a minute again the witness encircled certain parts of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree. The question is what he pointed at exactly. But perhaps he could combine these two questions, since the cooperation between the parties is -- You have -- you have been asked now by Ms. Mahindaratne where the Ukrainian Battalion was, and you -- one minute ago approximately you pointed at a certain part of what you indicated to be the Tito barracks, and that was, I would say, the wing that goes east-west on the northern side of the complex, just below where it reads "Put Zivota." Did you intend to indicate that the Ukrainian Battalion was stationed there had in that part of the complex?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was stationed here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness is now pointing at the western wing and the northern wing but only the western half of it. Do you have further questions, Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The map may be returned. I have only a couple of questions, Mr. President, to conclude cross-examination, contrary to what I indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're also distinguishing between your last and your very last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to avoid too much work for the you should and Madam Registrar, but I can see it's already too late, I would suggest that you retain possession of the maps. Could the usher please return. Could he approach us. [In English] Could you return the maps, please. And with your leave, of course, Mr. President, could you redistribute them to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have additional questions to that. Okay. You put your next questions, and meanwhile the maps can be redistributed again. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you testified that there was a 500-metres radius around the PTT building, on all four sides of the PTT building which was considered to be -- if I may use the word, safe zone?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a fence which demarcated that boundary line?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: No. There was no boundaries for the very 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there sandbags or some type of -- of something that demarcated that line, the 500-metre radius, from the outside area?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: In front of PTT direction to the road, there was a sandbag fence, where as far as I remember, there was a French checkpoint for incoming vehicle, just to -- to protect the area where passengers left cars, APCs, and so. But if I was looking from our window where we lived, and there was no fence -- I mean, this is 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your position, then, that there were guards -- you referred to the term "French officers," or -- "French checkpoint." You used the word "French checkpoint." Was there --

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Yes, it was a French checkpoint. There was just a corps company, a headquarter company who was responsible for guarding for everything concerning security of headquarter Sarajevo and PTT building itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the French checkpoint guarded the 500-metre radius around the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, actually, they guarded all the area which could be seen from their checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noticed that there might be some confusion. When you're talking about the French officers guarding, did you mean to say that they were guarding the 500-metre line, or were they guarding close to the building where approximately it goes to the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, they guarded all the area which they could observe, not only this 500 metres. 500 metres it was a special distance where warring parties couldn't be. But from the point of view of security, French guards, they guarded all situation around. And by the way, they had the one observation post on the roof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But how close were they to the building where they --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was some curve, approximately maybe -- maybe 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the French checkpoint positioned in such a way to observe the 500-metre radius around the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Yes, in places where it was possible, they observed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If a mortar or an artillery round was fired from outside this 500-metre radius, you would still hear the sound from the building; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, if I had that -- it depends where one was present at that time, was the window opened and many things which could affect and just to -- to define exactly the distance. But if there was a close outgoing fire, it was heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No more questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I have a certain number of questions. But first of all, could the witness be taken out of the courtroom. There is something I would like to say, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, will you please escort the witness out of the courtroom for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, I wanted to say that we should all respect the Rules and in particular the Prosecution with regard to your Chamber. I was quite shocked, but I didn't react so as not to waste any time and so as not to cause an incident in front of the witness -- I was shocked to see that the Prosecution did not hesitate to put its own positions in a state of perjury in order to guide the witness. My learned colleague presented this witness with an incident, said that if there was a shot, there was never smoke, and this was presented as a fact. If you remember - I can't check it here, because that was in another courtroom - throughout this process, when there is a tank firing in Sarajevo, the Prosecution would ask the witness to verify that fire had been opened from automatic weapons on this tank on the basis that one saw smoke coming out of the barrel, of the cannon. There were even scenes when one froze the image on the screen to ask the witness whether he saw smoke coming out of the weapon in order to try and obtain the response from the witness. And today one has presented as an affirmation the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first see. What part are you actually referring to, so I can better refer you to about smoke and --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if this has to do with the past, I can't do it. It was in another hearing that this happened. But the question is on page 53. It's page 53.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first see what is on page 53.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please refer to the words so it's quicker to get there. You said smoke was one of the words? Then I'll find the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's 53, Mr. President. I made a note of it. The witness said -- "it's evident."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please guide me more. I have the word "smoke." First I am looking for --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I read is: "If you consider that all these elements, the distances were the same with regard to an incoming round as well as an outgoing round, would you not agree with me that factors such as sound --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, Mr. President, when you're reading, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Would you not agree with me that factors such as sound, smoke, and the feel of the vibration assists one in monitoring or observing an incoming round much better than an outgoing round?" That is where I see "smoke" appearing in a question from the Prosecution. When I did understand your observation, which was put in rather strong words - if I do understand your observation well - you suggested that by asking this question, Ms. Mahindaratne suggested, and therefore as I did understand you well in this way, lured the witness almost into a perjury that -- she suggested that there would be no smoke to be noticed in an outgoing -- when the fire was outgoing --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Didn't she say that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I understood this question to be is that smoke, sound, and the feeling of vibration would give a better opportunity to observe incoming rounds than outgoing rounds. I did not understand, for example, that Ms. Mahindaratne suggested that it would make no noise. That's the reference to -- that's the sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: She has stated this. I am watching my words. That's what she stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. She said that there would be a better --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I disagree with you. [In English] -- There is no smoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, then I have it wrong. I did read a part -- and I would be highly appreciate it if you then would --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not the first time, Mr. President. That is something that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that's exactly the reason why I asked you to guide me to the PLACE you're referring to. I did read that part. I did read it slowly in order to give an opportunity to tell that I was reading the right or the wrong part. So I take it then that you would like to bring me to another part. Then please guide me further.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can find this on page 53, line 5. It's possible that my computer is not telling the truth. But if I am saying something and asking the witness to leave, I am not doing this for anyone's amusement, certainly not for that of your Chamber. And perhaps my words were very strong, but I was very clear that the Defence cannot admit that within the framework of these proceedings, things are being said on such important facts and then suddenly tables are turned and their position, the contrary is stated, while no one, in your Chamber included, no one reacts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just see. The line you just referred me to is page 53, line 5. Let me just first read and see what the context is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Mahindaratne, I have now seen you have asked in page 52 whether factors such as sound, smoke, and perhaps the field of vibration would be the factors that would assist an UNMO, whether that would be the case. The witness then answered: "Yes, of course." And then your next question reads in the transcript: "In the case of outgoing rounds, there's no smoke." And then the witness answers: "Obviously." Please respond, because that's the part we are dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this line of questioning was with regard to the discrepancy, if I may use that word --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- Between the incoming rounds and outgoing rounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Which was with regard to incoming mortar rounds and incoming artillery rounds. And clearly the witness has understood my line of questioning because he goes on to say - if I may draw your attention, Mr. President -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The initial question was: "Let me put it to you in a different way. In the case of incoming rounds, there are factors such as sound, smoke, and perhaps the field of vibration, which are factors that would assist UNMO to observe the incoming round. Isn't that the case?" And the witness not only answers, Mr. President, he goes on to say further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- He says: "Okay. Finally I've understood what you are asking me. Well, of course, for all this is three parameters, like smoke -- like just light when it's explosion and vibration. Of course it's more easily -- could be easily observed by anybody." Now, clearly in the case of mortars and artillery, there is no smoke when a round is fired. I think what Mr. Piletta-Zanin is referred to, in terms of the Prosecution's position with regard to being seen smoke at the point of firing is tank fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And it is certainly not a contradiction in terms of the position taken by the Prosecution. The line of questioning has been understood very well by the witness, and I cannot see why it cannot be understood by the learned Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I be heard, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that there are two words that I can see in English. We're speaking here about the outgoing and incoming rounds. And it is very clear that this question was asked in general about methods of observation. We know that there were several. There were different types of weapons. There's artillery, in the artillery. There are tanks that are used in different modes, and the same thing goes for anti-aircraft weapons. And I believe that this explanation is almost far fetched of -- the Prosecution stated contrary to what they had stated in the past, and we do not accept, and I don't think that the positions can be changed so much in the course of the proceedings unless this is clearly stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I do understand that you strongly oppose against the way Ms. Mahindaratne expressed herself. What procedural consequences do you think the Chamber should attach to it? Should the answer be struck because the witness was most -- I'm just trying to find out, apart from that you want to express your dissatisfaction with the way the -- Ms. Mahindaratne put her question, in your view, what else, apart from expressing your dissatisfaction, you'd like to Chamber to do about this? To strike the answer, to -- then we can take a decision, apart from having heard your -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you very much. But I believe that the Chamber should decide what they have to do. They have to look at what has been said prior to this in the framework of the questions that were asked by the Prosecution in relation to the rounds and when the smoke was mentioned regarding the outgoing fire; the first solution. The second solution: Everything that has to do with this question has to be stricken. And that solution is we have to make sure that this problem doesn't arise again, that this is stressed in particular, because this has very disagreeable consequences for the Defence and, of course, for General Galic; for everyone, in fact, inside and around this courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I propose that the learned Defence counsel produces the -- the portion of the transcript which he says is contradictory to the question that was put to this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with pleasure. But I have already said, and I believe that I am less and less understood and heard, I cannot do it because this hearing happened in another courtroom and we know that the recording of the transcript happening in one courtroom cannot be transferred to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just stop you. I did understand the request of Ms. Mahindaratne that you would indicate what part of today's transcript should be taken out, ignored, or not being part of the evaluation. That was, I think, what she asked you to indicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am leaving it up to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So your request is to strike out that part of the transcript that would be contaminated by this question. The Chamber will consider the matter and give a decision on your request.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I also propose that the learned counsel suggests that this portion is contradictory to a position taken by the Prosecution, that the portion of that transcript which is supposed to be contradictory to the question put to this witness has not been put forth, not indicated, even in terms of a page number. So let --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the -- the Defence could not do that ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. President, if I may just point out: Over the weekend, Mr. Piletta-Zanin could find the portion of the evidence led by -- or the question taken by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can -- here we find one of the disadvantages of the splitting up the tasks of the -- of the Prosecution. It's the recollection of the Chamber that evidence has been presented where on a video a tank appears from behind a building - I think it was a house - fires, and I think the Defence is pointing at that video image where it appears that smoke -- there's smoke. Whether there's firing, I don't know. But at least there was smoke, and the tank seems to have -- and then the tank is hiding again -- I think that's the part the Defence is referring to, and I think that there is no specific need, if you would look at the videos -- Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you very much, my learned colleague, that she's interested in my weekend professionally speaking. I believe that from memory I can say that the witness was quoted, but now we are going to check whether this was a protected witness. And I'm told yes. So in order not to make an error -- we believe that was -- that was Witness D, "D" as in "debate," Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just in the interest of time factor. If I may clearly point out my question related to mortars and artillery, because that was the larger part of the discrepancy between incoming rounds and outgoing rounds related to that, with regard to the documents that are shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If any of the parties would like to submit anything more - and I think I gave sufficient guidance to the Prosecution to identify the evidence is Defence is referring to - if any of the parties would add something to what has been said until now, they have an opportunity to do so in writing until next Monday by 12.00. The Chamber has heard the consequences the Defence considers to be appropriate to be attached to the objection they've made. The Chamber will then consider the matter and will give a decision on the request.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And one more question: I might have misunderstood you, Ms. Mahindaratne, where I said that you were asking the Defence to indicate what part of the transcript. I now -- my attention was drawn to the fact that you were actually asking the source of where it would have been the Prosecution's position that smoke did appear when firing a tank. But the second question would be that Mr. Piletta-Zanin left it to the Chamber, but the second question then was my question and not yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you very much for your position, and I take note, so I will not react during the weekend - perhaps later on, but I don't think so - but for the time being I'm going to have to ask certain questions about this aspect, regarding the smoke, and I'm going to do it at the same time not knowing what your -- the outcome will be, what your final position will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's just assume. Is there any difference in position as far as the Defence and the Prosecution are concerned that a tank firing produces some smoke?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Wouldn't it be the wisest thing then to do to put to the witness that where it has been said to him that outgoing fire would produce no smoke, that the Prosecution did not suggest with that that none of the weaponry mentioned would produce any smoke when firing and whether if adjusted in this way, the witness would have reason to change his answer. Would that be a solution that would --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I would say so. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what I am suggesting is that I can simply ask -- because this procedure shocked me a great deal -- I can perhaps ask a rather leading question of the witness whether weapons, AA, tanks, heavy machine-guns included in the artillery, whether they produced smoke, whether smoke was coming out of those barrels, and then we can conclude the rest. And the Defence is not absolutely certain that large-calibre mortars do not produce a little bit of smoke, when we know that some of them have propulsive discharges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then I take it that the answers to those questions should be considered by the Chamber, isn't it? Yes. Would it then still be necessary to take a decision on striking out the earlier answers? Because if they're contradicted, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence leaves it up to the authority of your Chamber, whatever the measures are to be taken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then try to resolve the matter in re-examination. The witness may be brought into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Re-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I apologise for this interruption. Earlier today you were asked one and even more than one question regarding the smoke that was produced or not produced by certain weapons when there are outgoing shots, outgoing rounds. I am now going to ask you some questions that, with the leave of everyone, perhaps could be slightly leading questions. Witness, weapons such as anti-aircraft cannons, tanks, heavy machine-guns, field guns, et cetera, these weapons, do they produce smoke at the moment when the round is fired? No matter how much there is of some smoke, but is there some smoke.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the use of the word "field guns, et cetera." These weapons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please answer the question in respect of the weaponry mentioned by Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what is concerning all the weapons mentioned are, first of all, we are -- I think the defender meant incoming. Or maybe I'm confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or maybe it's translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kruk, does an anti-aircraft cannon produce smoke even if only a small portion when firing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course not. It's -- actually anti-aircraft cannon, just will produce small fire in the muzzle. And it's -- they fire one by one or in bursts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the question was: Would they produce smoke, even if it would be little?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the same question for tanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For when outgoing fire doesn't produce smoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In tanks. Then heavy machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Field guns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you were asked about the sensations you could feel at the level of vibrations in the field, the physical vibrations and the sound you could hear and other sensations. The question I want to ask you has to do with the military observers, whether on the Lima or Papa side, were they close to monitored pieces. And in particular, when we are referring or if we are discussing outgoing fire.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: What does it mean "pieces"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. It was a translation error. Weapons. Pieces would refer to the battery.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or any other kind of weapon.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Most of these weapons, they were stationed in closed [Realtime transcript read in error "those"] positions. And in this case UNMOs could only hear the outgoing fire from these kind of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Just for the transcript, I wonder whether the witness said "those positions" or "closed positions."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we ask the witness to repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, closed positions, it means a weapon like mortar, like artillery. It's stationed on the closed position. It means it cannot be seen. It's a military term, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. President, it's closed position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in fact, these are positions the location of which you weren't aware of; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: You mean positions which UNMO were aware or -- because this questions referred to UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This still has to do with the observers. It's still in relation to the observers.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Of course they knew this approximate location of these positions, and that's why they could [Realtime transcript read in error "couldn't"] monitor when these kind of weapons were fired and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: As I recall, the witness said that's "why they could monitor" and it has been recorded as "couldn't monitor."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could, could, could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It has been rectified. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. And as a result, in relation to this question of whether it was close or not, did the observation units, the UN observation unit have the obligation of holding positions by the weapons in question -- the weapons in question?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: What does it mean "holding"? What does it mean to hold positions?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] To have people on site. Only to have people on site, next to the weapons. Still talking about UNMOs, of course. Was that an obligation; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Obligations to keep UNMOs next to these positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct. Next to the weapons.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, as far as -- as far as I remember, military observers were placed especially for their purpose to monitor cease-fire violations. It means outgoing/incoming fire. And the positions were chosen to have a possibility to monitor as much as possible territory which were -- which led just from observation post. But as well, it was taken in consideration that these observation posts were not so close to -- to confrontation line and to positions which existed at that time on confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Witness, can you remind us - because we're always discussing the matter of positions - how many positions were there, as far as you know, in terms of the Papa and the Lima position, as far as your stay there is concerned, during that period?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And with the assistance of the usher, we could put the map on the ELMO in order to save time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is not a matter that arose in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I respond briefly. I think it did, because the problem is as follows. We're talking about physical sensations and visual sensations. Obviously if there are many places next to the weapons, this is understandable. But if it's all dispersed, it's less understandable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we -- I don't know what the purpose of this question is. We heard evidence on where the Papa and Lima observation posts were very specific in certain parts of time. It's not my recollection that there was great disagreement between the parties on the positions of the Papa and Lima observation posts during that time. So therefore, I wonder whether -- unless --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a difference with regard to one point. One of the points it changed. But I don't want to talk about this in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't think that it arises out from cross-examination to go through positions of all the Lima posts. But if -- of course, if it would be of any assistance for any of your next questions, then we could just ask whether he knows where they were and then put the next question and just assume that where this 95 per cent agreement -- Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you answer the question, such as it has been phrased, and first with regard to Papa.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, the situation was as follows: We had five Papas placed in different parts of the city. And what is concerning Lima: They actually reported in a different way. I can explain why, because sometimes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. First the question was whether you were aware of where these observation posts --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You know that. Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of your answer, witness, and bearing in mind what you yourself answered, with regard to the traces of smoke, the flashes, et cetera, from these five Papa posts was it possible to have a global view on all the sides of the town -- of all the sides of the town, including the sides of buildings? And when I say "global," I mean the totality.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, I can say that I don't think it was possible to cover all the areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll stop you there. This is why I asked you my question. If, for example, there is a shot which intervenes on the side -- which happens on the side of a facade which is not visible and at a certain distance from a Papa post or Papa posts, what is the sensation that allows you to report on its existence, if of course there are any such elements, since you can't see a flash and you can't see any smoke?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: I think we returned the same situation as it was before. From one point -- at that time I was an ops officer but not UNMO. Of course you are right. If you cannot see the light when explosion just hit the ground or something, you cannot -- well, you can see some black smoke, but it depends on many things as well, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I have to stop you. I've got the gist of your answer. My question is as follows. And I'm now referring to mortars, to mortar shells. This type of a mortar, does it produce a lot of smoke, not very much smoke, or whatever, when it explodes?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It produces smoke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question was: A lot or a little?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: It depends on the calibre of mortar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. This will be my very last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we put the map on the ELMO again, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said that the logistics section that you reported to was, and I quote: [In English] "Next to UN camp." [Interpretation] That is to say, right next to the installation in question. You mentioned the rail. Could you tell us where this separation fence was located, if you know anything about this. Could you tell us roughly.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Here was, I believe, our --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object. I'm sorry. I came in a little late. The witness did not report that there was a logistic section. He only merely said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, we have been talking about a logistic section of which we all know that the witness heard that it was there and that he was told what the position of that base was that was behind the fence. So let's just hear whether there's any further information and whether there might have been something else there that -- we do not know yet. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Could you simply answer the question, because I didn't hear that. Would you be capable of pinpointing on this map very roughly the position of the fence that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, the building was divided just two ways: This way and this way. And here somewhere was the end of UN camp, somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And the separation line, the fence itself, did it continue in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, actually, that area, where was the fence, there was a storage place for battalion, and I actually -- maybe I went there once. That's why -- I don't remember details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, with regard to your visits, you stated that you went there three or four times. It doesn't really matter how many times. I'd like to know whether when you went there, perhaps later, do you know if there were any exchanges of fire in that zone?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Well, when I was -- when I visited battalion at that time, I heard only from the territory of this battalion some -- a few explosions, and most of information I had from Ukrainian officers or from daily situation report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you know whether there were any exchanges of fire in the zone, small arms?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Yes. According to reports of our battalion, there was some exchange of fire, some shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For the sake of the transcript, I refer to where the witness is pointing at when he indicated where the fence would have been. He was pointing at the northern wing of what he indicated to be the Tito barracks, approximately in the middle of that wing. And may I ask you just for one clarification of your last answer: When you said your exchange of fire, it was reported in one of the questions that said when you heard exchange of fire when you were there. Could you please clarify on whether, apart from exchange of fire being reported, that there had also been exchange of fire when you visited the battalion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I visited battalion, I didn't hear any exchange of fire. I heard some explosions but not -- not very close to location of our battalion. It was actually somewhere on some distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one question for you, Mr. Kruk. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said that when you were on your engineering mission that once small arm fire took place, that very soon retaliation by a mortar took place. Could you tell us what you understood to be "very soon." How much time elapsed approximately between the fire from small arms and the retaliation by mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: ANATOLIY KRUK
utterances.text: Maybe 10, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Mr. Kruk -- and I don't think this causes any questions. Mr. Kruk, this concludes your evidence in this court. You've answered many questions from the parties and there was only one question from the Bench. Nevertheless, we thank you for having answered all our questions, and we'd like to wish you a safe journey home again. We will adjourn until next Monday. We are sitting again in -- Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, still the Prosecution has no indication as to the schedule of witnesses for next week. The fact that, in fact, DP2 is coming on Tuesday and not Monday was also indicated when I raised that issue this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we could deal with these matters not -- I mean, there's nothing against the presence of the witness, but I don't know whether he's that much interested to hear our procedural issues. So Mr. Usher, would you please escort Mr. Kruk out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's only this morning when I -- there was this issue as to what would happen when DP2 comes on Monday that we were informed that in fact DP2 will be coming only on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So we would be thankful if the Defence could indicate and give us notice of the schedule of witnesses for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence provided the Prosecution with a submission in good time in which it said which witnesses would be appearing next week. I am now trying to see whether I have brought that submission with me, but I am sure that I informed them. And according to the schedule, given the current situation, on Monday we were to continue with examining Bukva Milorad and then Milenko Indjic on Monday, but DP2 is also a witness who should be examined that week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the names you just mentioned are not protected or there's not sought any protection for them?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The letter learned counsel is referring to does not indicate as to who's coming when. Just the names have been given in a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With whom are we starting next Monday, Ms. Pilipovic? Is it in the order you indicated just when you read the names?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the only possibility, since the witnesses are here. But I'll provide this today. I'll provide the time and the schedule, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the remainder of the week, the witness suggests Sinisa Krsman and Sasa Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In respect of this list, did we receive summaries or are they separate? Ms. Pilipovic, perhaps we'll go into private session for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
